items.stem: Why does randomly assigning users to control and treatment support a causal conclusion?

options.text: Randomization balances confounders on average, so outcome differences are attributable to the treatment
options.rationale: Correct: random assignment makes the groups comparable except for the treatment.

options.text: It guarantees the sample is representative of all users
options.rationale: Randomization balances groups against each other; it does not ensure population representativeness.

options.text: It removes the need for a control group
options.rationale: A control group is still required for comparison.

options.text: It makes the p-value always significant
options.rationale: Randomization does not control significance, which depends on effect and sample size.

items.explanation: Correct: random assignment makes the groups comparable except for the treatment.

items.stem: Which statements about experiment analysis are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Repeatedly checking results and stopping when significant inflates the false-positive rate
options.rationale: Correct: peeking without correction increases spurious significant findings.

options.text: A statistically significant lift may still be too small to matter in practice
options.rationale: Correct: statistical and practical significance are distinct.

options.text: A non-significant result proves the treatment has no effect
options.rationale: It fails to detect an effect; it does not prove none exists.

options.text: Testing many metrics needs no adjustment for multiple comparisons
options.rationale: Multiple comparisons require adjustment to control false positives.

items.explanation: Correct: peeking without correction increases spurious significant findings.; Correct: statistical and practical significance are distinct.

items.stem: What does statistical power describe in an experiment?

options.text: The probability of detecting a true effect of a given size if it exists
options.rationale: Correct: power is the chance of correctly rejecting the null when the effect is real.

options.text: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
options.rationale: Power is not the probability the null is true.

options.text: The size of the observed effect
options.rationale: Effect size is separate from power.

options.text: The significance threshold chosen for the test
options.rationale: That is alpha, the false-positive rate, not power.

items.explanation: Correct: power is the chance of correctly rejecting the null when the effect is real.
